old: Read this slowly into a recorder, speak it aloud, or learn its movement and use silent words if that comes easily. Choose one anchor—a sound, bodily contact, or your two-hand practice—and an opening phrase. Keep using the same anchor where the words refer to it. Pause between paragraphs; don’t read the delivery directions aloud.
new: Guide to self-guided Silent Contact Practise reading it slowly into a recorder, or reading it aloud or (best if you can manage it) learning it and saying the words to yourself silently. Choose to use sound or bodily contact or two hands throughout and choose an opening phrase. Whenever the guide mentions ‘the anchor’ use your chosen anchor and pause at the end of each paragraph for a few moments. (Don’t say aloud any of the instructions about how to do the reading.)

old: Let your eyes settle somewhere in the room, somewhere they can rest for a little while, and notice the difference between looking for something and letting what is already there come into view.
new: Pause, and let your eyes rest somewhere in the room.

old: There is a surface beneath you. Notice where you meet it … the contact, the pressure, whatever you can actually feel. And while you notice that, a sound may reach you, or a breath may draw your attention, without needing you to arrange either one.
new: Now as you notice where you are resting on the surface beneath you, notice the feel of that contact, and notice also a sound or your breathing.

old: You can give this a little time.
new: There’s all the time in the world to do this.

old: A thought about the day may still be here. A thought about whether you’re doing this properly may be here too. There is room to notice a thought and return to the anchor you chose, without finishing the thought first.
new: If there’s a thought in there, perhaps about something from your day, or even about what you’re doing now, see if you can turn your attention to the anchor even if there is a thought there.

old: And as you return, you may find one detail that holds your interest … something about the sound, or the contact, or that particular way of listening … and let attention stay with it long enough to become curious.
new: See if you can find a way of listening to the sound or the contact (or to your listening) that captures your interest in some detail.

old: Perhaps you can give yourself the time you would give someone you care about who has begun to speak and hasn’t yet found the words. You can remain nearby, listening, without finishing their sentence for them.
new: Give yourself as much time for this as you would for someone close to you who was trying to speak to you.

old: Let your chosen phrase come to mind now. Say it as an invitation, and notice how it is received.
new: Now perhaps say or think to yourself your chosen phrase, and notice how it is received.

old: As you continue, your eyes can close, soften, or stay open. Let that be a choice you make. Listening may deepen while a sound from the room remains available in the background.
new: You can close your eyes now if you wish, or soften them, or keep proceeding with them open. Deepen your listening now, keeping in the background the sound you chose.

old: Count slowly from five to one. Give each number its own moment.
new: Count slowly to yourself from 5 down to 1.

old: Five. Notice your chosen anchor again. Four. Let attention gather around what you find. Three. Leave a little space after the words. Two. Listen into that space, without preparing an answer. One. Stay here for a moment.
new: 5 Notice again your chosen anchor for today, 4 notice what you notice, 3, 2 listen into the space after these words 1 and stay here for a moment.

old: Bring your chosen concern lightly to mind, or remain with your wish for contact. Let it be present without rehearsing its whole story.
new: Now perhaps briefly bring to mind the concern you chose to work with, or just your wish to make contact.

old: What am I noticing now?
new: What do you notice?

old: Give the response time to take its own form. It might be a sensation, a few words, an image, a feeling, or an impulse to move. There may be nothing clear yet.
new: Give yourself time to notice what comes, be it sensations, words, images, feelings, urges to move or nothing.

old: Leave room to notice, with words or without them.
new: Give yourself time to notice this, with or without words.

old: Dishonest reframing declares that the problem was secretly good all along. I prefer questions that widen meaning without lying:
“What else might be true?” “What is this part trying to do for me?” “What would the Nurturer, the Protector, and the Leader each say about this?”
new: When I'm trying to reframe something, and I find that I'm doing it dishonestly, it's usually because I'm trying to convince myself that the issue or problem is actually a good thing. Some other questions that I might ask myself are: What else might be true here? What else might this be about? How might my Nurturer reframe this? How might my Protector reframe this? How might my Leader reframe this? And so on.

old: Advertising, fear, craving, screens, tribe, resentment, authority, loneliness, and repetition are already training the mind. Self-hypnosis lets you practice from inside it: befriending the deeper layers, listening closely, and making adult choice more available.
new: As you're certainly aware there are many, many forces at work in the world that are trying to train your mind in ways that benefit them. With self-hypnosis you can do much of the same thing from the inside, by befriending and communicating with the deeper part of your mind. This opens up a whole new area of choice for you as an adult in the world.

old: Use self-hypnosis as a relationship with yourself. When the situation needs actual care, the guide shouldn’t become a substitute for it.
new: Please keep in mind that this is a guide to self-hypnosis; it is about a relationship you have with yourself. In some cases it is appropriate to seek support for the situation you are facing, but this guide is not it.

old: Get urgent help now for immediate danger, severe confusion, inability to keep yourself safe, or concerning physical symptoms such as chest pain or fainting. New or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe insomnia, mania-like or psychosis-like symptoms, or dissociation that disrupts functioning need prompt professional assessment, not a four-to-twelve-week practice schedule.
new: You should get help now if you are in imminent danger, if you are very confused, if you cannot ensure your own safety, and/or if you are experiencing physical symptoms (e.g., chest pain, fainting, etc). You should also seek professional help promptly if you are experiencing new or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe insomnia, new or worsening manic or psychotic symptoms, or if dissociative symptoms are impacting your ability to function. These are not the types of things you should expect to resolve in 4-12 weeks by following a guide.
